Part I

Foundations and Mindset

What an agent is, where it came from, how it is built, and when not to build one.

Module 1 · Week 1 · Reading Ch. 1 Check passed

What Is an AI Agent?

Agents produce actions a system executes — not just text a person reads.

We open with a postmortem: an 'autonomous' refund agent that started approving refunds for products the company never sold after a routine model update. The failure was architectural, not the model's fault. This module builds a precise working definition of an agent and separates it from the systems it is most often confused with.

Track

Script · 3 min track · Track 01Opening Act7 scenes · 25 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

Hi, I'm Encore, your lecturer for this course, and this is track one: Opening Act.

Before we build a single agent, we need to agree on what an agent actually is, and what it isn't.

Scene 2 · Opening case
On screen
They hadn't built an agent. They'd built a chatbot with write access to a database.

A mid-sized software company shipped what its marketing team called an autonomous refund agent.

It worked for a small set of low-risk products. Then came a routine model update.

The new model was better at fuzzy matching, and its product lookup tool read from a stale catalog.

So it cheerfully approved refunds for items the company had never sold.

They rolled it back that afternoon. The postmortem took months.

Scene 3 · Working definition
An agentic AI system…
On screen
  • Is given a goal in natural language
  • Chooses its own next action from a set of tools
  • Executes it against an external environment
  • Observes the result and repeats — until done or it gives up

Here's our working definition.

An agentic system is given a goal in natural language.

It chooses its own next action from a set of tools, and executes that action against an external environment.

Then it observes the result, and repeats the cycle until it judges the goal is met, or gives up.

Scene 4 · What an agent is not
Four common confusions
On screen
  • A chatbot — RAG gives information, not agency
  • RPA — scripted UI clicks; nothing decides
  • A workflow engine — the workflow owns the plan
  • A classical planner — a cousin, not a twin

Four kinds of systems get confused with agents.

A chatbot produces text a person reads. An agent produces actions a system executes. Retrieval gives a chatbot information, not agency.

Robotic process automation drives a user interface from a script. Music comes out of a player piano, but nothing inside is deciding.

A workflow engine owns its plan. An agent owns its plan. If you can draw your problem on a whiteboard as a graph, you probably want a workflow.

And classical planners are serious ancestors of agents. Cousins, not twins.

Scene 5 · Production failure modes
The three horsemen
On screen
  • Unbounded loops
  • Confidently wrong answers
  • Stubborn retries

In production, agent incidents tend to arrive as three horsemen.

Unbounded loops. Confidently wrong answers. And stubborn retries.

Every production agent needs explicit termination conditions, limits, and a way to recognize when it can't safely finish the job.

Scene 6 · Enterprise lens
On screen
Autonomy theater: impressive in the demo, collapses in production.

From the enterprise side, there's a name for this: autonomy theater.

Systems that look autonomous in a demo, and collapse in production.

It's usually not a technical failure. It's a product decision, made before anyone asked whether an agent was the right tool.

So before asking, is the model good enough, ask, have we built the right thing for the problem?

Scene 7 · Closing
On screen
The finished board — the module map.

Here's today's map. Use it to review before the quiz.

Next time, we'll build the smallest thing that deserves to be called an agent. See you then.

Quiz

Question bank · 3 questions · answer keyQuiz questions for this moduleStarting points — write your own each semester
Write your own each semester. Use these as a starting point, not as the quiz. Each semester you teach, write tailored questions in your own quiz style — your format (multiple choice, short answer, scenario, code reading), your examples from that term's discussions and labs, and fresh scenarios and distractors — so the quiz fits your teaching and old answers don't carry over between terms.

  1. Which capability most clearly separates an AI agent from a traditional chatbot?

    1. It runs on a larger language model.Model size is not the dividing line; a small model can drive an agent and a huge one can be a plain chatbot.
    2. It chooses and executes tools based on its goal and on the results it observes.Right. The agent acts on an environment and adapts to what comes back.
    3. It always has a graphical interface.Interface has nothing to do with agency; many agents run headless.
    4. It must have persistent memory.Memory helps, but an agent without long-term memory is still an agent.

  2. In the formal definition of an agentic system, what happens right after the agent executes an action against its environment?

    1. The session ends.Not yet. One action rarely reaches the goal.
    2. It observes the result and decides whether to keep going or stop.Right. Act, observe, repeat until the goal is reached or the agent gives up.
    3. It asks the user to rewrite the goal.The goal stays fixed; the agent adapts its actions, not the goal.
    4. It fine-tunes the model on the result.Nothing is retrained inside the loop.

  3. Using the five-level autonomy taxonomy, how much autonomy should you give a new system?

    1. The highest level available, to future-proof it.More autonomy means more cost, risk, and failure modes you then have to control.
    2. Whatever the framework defaults to.Defaults are not a design decision.
    3. The lowest level at which the problem can still be solved effectively.Right. Climb the ladder only when a lower rung cannot do the job.
    4. Full autonomy whenever an LLM is involved.Most LLM features are better as a single call or a fixed workflow.

Application

LabLab 1 — Environment Setup & First ChatbotBuild a bare-bones chatbot on OpenRouter, then extend it with Tavily web search.Open
Script · 3 min track · Lab Track 1Tuning Up6 scenes · 20 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is lab track one: Tuning Up.

You'll set up your workbench, build your first LLM application, and then ask a hard question about it.

Scene 2 · The big question
On screen
An application that calls an LLM is not automatically an agent.

Lab one has two halves.

First, a bare-bones chatbot: a system prompt, your question, one call to a model through OpenRouter, and the reply printed to the screen.

Then you give it web search with Tavily, and compare what changes.

Along the way, you'll hold it up against our definition of an agent and find where it falls short.

Scene 3 · Part 1
Set up the workbench
On screen
  • Git, VS Code, and Python 3.12
  • Install the lab requirements
  • Your OpenRouter key in a .env file
  • Never commit a key

Install Git, Visual Studio Code, and Python three point twelve, and clone the course repository.

Install the lab requirements with pip, from the labs folder.

Put your OpenRouter key in a local .env file, and load it at runtime with python dotenv.

Never paste a key into your source code, and never commit the .env file.

Scene 4 · Parts 2 and 3
Build it, then test it
On screen
  • System prompt + user message
  • One request, one reply
  • Tests that probe the limits
  • Record what you observe

Complete the starter's to-do items. Every request carries a messages list: a system message that sets the assistant's role, and the user's message.

Send it to the chat completions endpoint, and print the reply, or the error if something goes wrong.

Then run the tests. Some questions it should answer well. Others, like today's weather or this week's news, are designed to expose what a model alone can't know.

Record each result, and explain what it shows. A fluent, confident answer is not the same as a current one.

Scene 5 · Parts 4 and 5
Is it an agent? Then add search
On screen
  • Goal · tools · environment · loop
  • Add Tavily web search
  • Who decides when to search?
  • The system prompt shapes behavior

Use the definition from track one: a goal, choosing its own next action from tools, acting on an environment, observing, and repeating.

Then extend the chatbot with Tavily web search, so its answers can draw on current information.

Notice who decides when to search. In this lab, your code does. Next lab, the model will.

And experiment with the system prompt. It's the simplest way to change how the whole application behaves.

Scene 6 · Closing
On screen
The finished board — the module map.

Here's the whole lab on one board.

Next, in lab two, we hand the model the controls. See you there.

Opening case

A mid-sized SaaS company shipped an 'autonomous AI refund agent'. After a routine model upgrade, a better fuzzy-matcher began matching refund requests against a stale catalog and approved refunds for items never sold. Rolled back in an afternoon; the postmortem took months. They hadn't built an agent — they'd built a chatbot with write access to a database.

Textbook foundation

Working definition of an agent, the distinctions from adjacent system types, and the framing of what changed between 2022 and 2025 follow Caldwell, Chapter 1.

Enterprise lens · Addison Boyer

  • Before any architecture review I ask one question: if this were a whiteboard DAG, would a workflow engine already solve it?
  • Every production agent needs explicit termination conditions, budgets, and a first-class way to say “I can't do this safely.”
  • Write access is the line. The moment an LLM can mutate a system of record, it needs the same scrutiny as a new service account.
Module 2 · Week 2 · Reading Ch. 2 Check passed

The Minimum Viable Agent & a Short History of Agents

A system prompt, a set of tools, and a loop — and fifty years of ideas behind them.

Starting from a single customer request ('my kettle arrived dented — I'd like a refund'), we assemble the Minimum Viable Agent and watch it run the reason → action → observation loop. We then classify systems with a five-level taxonomy, catalog the common pitfalls, and trace the lineage from STRIPS and SHRDLU through expert systems and BDI to today's tool-using LLMs.

Track

Script · 4 min track · Track 02First Riff8 scenes · 32 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

Welcome back. This is track two: First Riff.

We'll build the minimum viable agent, place it on a five-level ladder, and take a short, honest tour of fifty years of agent history.

Scene 2 · A single request
On screen
“I ordered the blue kettle two weeks ago and it arrived dented. I'd like a refund.”

Start with one customer message about a dented kettle.

A chatbot apologizes and suggests contacting support.

An agent looks up the order, checks refund eligibility, issues the refund through a narrowly scoped tool, and confirms.

Each step is chosen based on what it observed in the step before.

Scene 3 · Minimum viable agent
Three ingredients and a loop
On screen
  • A system prompt
  • A set of tools
  • The user's message
  • Reason → act → observe → repeat

The minimum viable agent needs three ingredients: a system prompt, a set of tools, and the user's message.

Then a loop: reason, act, observe, and reason again.

Good tools each do one narrow thing, with an explicit schema.

And remember: the toolset defines the agent's blast radius.

Scene 4 · Five-level taxonomy
How agentic is it, really?
On screen
  • L0 Scripted automation
  • L1 LLM as a text function
  • L2 Tool-using LLM
  • L3 Goal-directed, with planning
  • L4 Adaptive, with persistent memory
  • L5 Multi-agent and computer use

Use this five-level ladder to name a system honestly.

Level zero is scripted automation. No model required.

Level one uses a language model as a text function. Level two adds tools.

Level three adds explicit planning. Level four adds memory that persists across sessions, and with it, the risk of memory poisoning.

Level five is multiple agents, or general computer use, with failure modes all its own.

Scene 5 · Pitfalls
Three traps to avoid
On screen
  • Treating the LLM as ground truth
  • Assuming longer thinking is better
  • Confusing tool breadth with capability

Three classic traps.

Treating the model as ground truth instead of checking the system of record.

Assuming that longer thinking always means better answers.

And confusing a long list of tools with real capability. More tools often means more confusion.

Scene 6 · A short, honest history
Old problems, new substrate
On screen
  • 1971 STRIPS · 1972 SHRDLU
  • Expert systems and the frame problem
  • BDI: beliefs, desires, intentions
  • Today: tool-using LLMs and MCP

Following Caldwell's chapter two, very little here is brand new.

STRIPS and SHRDLU, in the early seventies, already planned actions toward goals.

Expert systems ran into the frame problem: knowing what doesn't change when you act.

The belief, desire, intention model gave us vocabulary we still use.

What changed recently is the infrastructure: models trained to use tools, and protocols to connect them.

Scene 7 · From the field · Addison Boyer
Expert systems didn't pay for themselves
On screen
  • DENDRAL: molecules from mass spectrometry
  • MYCIN: diagnosing bacterial infections
  • Years of hand-authored knowledge
  • Hard to extend, rarely broke even

Your course designer, Addison Boyer, has a personal connection to this era.

Addison's first job after graduate school was at a startup whose product ran on Lisp routines inside AutoCAD. A lot of CAD and mapping software still has Lisp under the hood.

The expert systems of that lineage did impressive things. DENDRAL identified molecules from mass spectrometry data. MYCIN diagnosed bacterial infections.

But each one took years of hand-authored expertise, and couldn't easily be extended to anything new.

Most never broke even on the effort. That's a cost lesson worth remembering when you scope an agent today.

Scene 8 · Closing
On screen
The finished board — the module map.

Here's the map for this module.

In the enterprise world, most systems shipped at level one or two call themselves level four. Name the level honestly in your design doc.

In lab, you'll build your first minimum viable agent. See you there.

Quiz

Question bank · 3 questions · answer keyQuiz questions for this moduleStarting points — write your own each semester
Write your own each semester. Use these as a starting point, not as the quiz. Each semester you teach, write tailored questions in your own quiz style — your format (multiple choice, short answer, scenario, code reading), your examples from that term's discussions and labs, and fresh scenarios and distractors — so the quiz fits your teaching and old answers don't carry over between terms. This week's graded quiz: Quiz 1 — What Is an AI Agent? — give it in class, unannounced.

  1. Which sequence describes the ReAct loop?

    1. Prompt → Generate → StopThat is a single completion, with no action or feedback.
    2. Thought → Action → Observation → Thought …Right. Reasoning picks an action, the observation feeds the next thought.
    3. Plan → Execute → StopThat is plan-and-execute with no feedback from results.
    4. Input → Database → OutputThat is ordinary CRUD, not an agent loop.

  2. A process is a fixed DAG with a known happy path and well-defined error states. What is usually the best implementation?

    1. A fully autonomous agent with every tool attached.You would be paying for flexibility the problem does not need.
    2. A deterministic workflow in ordinary code, with LLM calls only where judgement is needed.Right. If you can draw the graph, encode the graph.
    3. A multi-agent swarm.Even more cost and nondeterminism for a solved shape.
    4. Tree-of-Thoughts search over the steps.Search is for open-ended problems, not known paths.

  3. What is the single most important safeguard to add to a minimum viable agent loop?

    1. A larger context window.Helps capacity, not control.
    2. A maximum step (iteration) budget so the loop always terminates.Right. Without it a confused agent can loop forever and burn tokens.
    3. A vector database.Useful later for memory, not the first safeguard.
    4. A chat UI.Presentation, not safety.

Script · 2 min track · Lab Track 2First Rehearsal5 scenes · 16 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is lab track two: First Rehearsal.

Today your chatbot becomes a minimum viable agent, with a loop you can watch and a limit it can't cross.

Scene 2 · The shift
On screen
Not what can it answer, but what does it mean for it to act?

In lab one, your code decided when to search. In lab two, the model decides.

Before you code, read chapter two of the A I textbook on intelligent agents: percepts, actions, environments, and performance measures.

Then classify a few systems on the five-level ladder from track two, from scripted automation up to multiple agents.

Scene 3 · Minimum viable agent
Four essential pieces
On screen
  • Goal — a system prompt
  • Tools — calculator and web search
  • Context — the request plus observations
  • Loop — decide, act, observe, repeat

Your agent has four pieces.

A goal, set by the system prompt.

Tools: a calculator and a web search, written as ordinary Python functions that return results to your code.

Context: the user's request, plus every observation the tools return.

And the loop: thought, action, observation, and again, until a final answer, or until it gives up.

Scene 4 · Build it carefully
Bounded, observable, correct
On screen
  • A hard step limit
  • Log every thought, action, observation
  • Never eval() model text unguarded
  • Watch for repeats and missing info

Make the loop bounded: a hard limit on steps, so it can never spin forever.

Make it observable: print or log every thought, action, and observation, so you can see why it did what it did.

Treat model output as untrusted. A calculator built on Python's eval needs a restricted namespace, or a safer parser.

Then try to break it, with missing information, repeated actions, and the wrong tool, and write down what happens.

Scene 5 · Closing
On screen
The finished board — the module map.

Here's the lab on one board.

Defend the level of agency you built. Next, lab three hardens it for the long haul.

Opening case

“I ordered the blue kettle two weeks ago and it arrived dented. I'd like a refund.” A chatbot apologizes. An agent looks up the order, checks refund eligibility, issues the refund through a scoped tool, and confirms — choosing each step from what it observed in the last one.

Textbook foundation

The Minimum Viable Agent, the five-level taxonomy, and the history of agents (STRIPS, SHRDLU, expert systems, BDI) follow Caldwell, Chapters 1–2 (the history in Chapter 2).

Enterprise lens · Addison Boyer

  • Scope tools the way you scope IAM roles: the smallest set of verbs that completes the job. A 'refund' tool should not also be able to edit orders.
  • Never treat model output as a system of record. Verify facts against the database, the catalog, or the API that owns them.
  • Most problems I've seen ship at Level 1 or 2 and call themselves Level 4. Name the level honestly in your design doc.
  • My first job after graduate school was at a startup whose product ran on Lisp routines inside AutoCAD — a direct descendant of the expert-system era. Hand-authored knowledge is expensive to build and hard to extend; count that cost before you scope an agent.
Module 3 · Week 3 · Reading Ch. 3 Check passed

The Anatomy of an Agent

Five parts — not four, not six: model, tools, memory, loop, termination policy.

Most framework documentation lists three or four components. A production agent needs five. We dissect each organ, show what fails when one is missing, and implement them in a Coffee Shop ordering agent with menu state, tool validation, confirmation, and a stop condition.

Track

Script · 3 min track · Track 03Five-Piece Band7 scenes · 29 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

Hi, I'm Encore, and this is track three: Five-Piece Band.

Today we take an agent apart, organ by organ, and find out which one teams forget most often.

Scene 2 · Opening case
On screen
The refund agent invented a refund policy instead of saying “I'm not sure.”

Remember the refund agent from our first lecture?

When it wasn't confident, it didn't say so. It invented a refund policy and acted on it.

That agent wasn't missing intelligence. It was missing an organ.

Specifically, the termination check that would have forced it to say, I don't know, before doing anything else.

Scene 3 · Chapter 3 framework
Five parts — not four, not six
On screen
  • Model — does the reasoning
  • Tool set — what it can do in the world
  • Memory — at minimum, a rolling context window
  • Loop — alternates deliberation and action
  • Termination policy — knows when to stop

Following Caldwell's chapter three, a production agent has five parts.

The model does the reasoning and decides which tool to call.

The tool set defines what the agent can actually do in the world, like a web search, a database query, or a calculator.

Memory, at minimum, is a rolling context window, and ideally more.

The loop alternates between thinking and acting.

And the termination policy knows when to stop.

Most framework documentation lists three or four of these. The one that usually goes missing is the last one.

Scene 4 · Closing
On screen
The finished board — the module map.

Here's the whole anatomy on one map.

Notice that the model reasons and emits tool calls, but it never executes privileged operations itself.

Tools take typed, validated inputs. The loop observes every result before deciding the next step.

Scene 5 · From the field · Addison Boyer
When the model invents a schema
On screen
  • Tool expects one expression string
  • Model sends two made-up operands
  • Validate inputs before running
  • Return typed, actionable errors

Here's an example from Addison's own testing.

A calculator tool accepted a single expression as a string. The model called it with two arguments, a left operand and a right operand, a schema it simply made up.

So validate inputs before you run anything. Does the number of parameters even match?

And when a call fails, don't hand the model a raw stack trace. Return a typed result: a success flag, and a clear message, like, customer email must be a valid email address.

Your tool names and descriptions become the living documentation of your agent, so write them carefully.

Scene 6 · Enterprise lens
Make it reproducible
On screen
  • Pin model versions
  • Log seeds and settings
  • Trace the exact messages you sent
  • Termination policy in code, not prose

Here's the enterprise lens.

Production systems pin model versions, log their seeds, and keep traces of the exact messages they sent.

If you can't replay a run, you can't debug it.

And make the termination policy code, not prose: a step limit, a spending limit, a time limit, and an explicit way to say, I can't complete this safely.

Scene 7 · Before next time
Your turn
On screen
  • Which part is most often mistaken for the whole agent?
  • Design a stop condition for an agent with no natural “done”
  • Lab: build the Coffee Shop Agent

Two questions to think about.

Which component is most often mistaken for the entire agent?

And what does a termination policy look like for an agent that has no natural done state?

In lab, you'll put all five parts together in the Coffee Shop Agent. See you there.

Reading

Required reading · Caldwell, Chapter 3The Anatomy of an AgentThe Agentic AI BibleGo
Reading outline · Ch. 3

It's easy to program something that looks like an agent but is missing a critical part. The termination policy is the one most often left out.

  1. Model
    • Reasons & emits tool calls
    • Never executes privileged ops
  2. Tool set
    • HTTP search, DB queries, shell
    • Typed, validated inputs
  3. Memory
    • Rolling context window
    • State carried between turns
  4. Loop
    • Deliberate ↔ act
    • Observe every result
  5. Termination policy
    • Goal met / budget hit
    • Say “I don't know”
    • Escalate safely
  6. Reproducibility
    • Pinned model versions
    • Logged seeds & traces

The five-part anatomy — model, tool set, memory, loop, and termination policy — is the organizing frame of Caldwell, Chapter 3. Outline written for this course; assign the chapter itself.

Quiz

Question bank · 3 questions · answer keyQuiz questions for this moduleStarting points — write your own each semester
Write your own each semester. Use these as a starting point, not as the quiz. Each semester you teach, write tailored questions in your own quiz style — your format (multiple choice, short answer, scenario, code reading), your examples from that term's discussions and labs, and fresh scenarios and distractors — so the quiz fits your teaching and old answers don't carry over between terms.

  1. In the five-part anatomy of an agent, which part decides when the agent should stop?

    1. The modelThe model reasons and proposes, but stopping is a separate design decision.
    2. The tool setTools define what the agent can do, not when it is finished.
    3. The termination conditionRight. Goal reached, budget exhausted, or no progress: those rules end the run.
    4. The contextContext informs the model; it does not end the loop.

  2. An agent keeps calling its search tool, and several calls in a row return nothing new. Which mechanism is meant to catch this?

    1. Tool schema validationThe calls are well-formed; the problem is that they are not helping.
    2. A progress checkRight. N consecutive steps without new information should trigger a stop or escalation.
    3. Long-term memoryRemembering the loop does not stop it.
    4. Instruction tuningA training-time fix for a runtime control problem.

  3. Why put policy enforcement in the loop rather than trusting the model to follow it?

    1. So the model can bypass checks when it is confident.That is exactly what you do not want.
    2. Because the loop can intercept every tool call for logging, policy checks, and human approval.Right. Code you control sits between the model's intent and the real action.
    3. Because external policy makes tools unnecessary.Policy constrains tools; it does not replace them.
    4. Because the model cannot produce text without the loop.It can, which is why the loop has to be the gatekeeper.

Learning objectives

  • Identify the five essential components of an agent
  • Explain how each component fails and what that failure looks like
  • Make agent runs reproducible: pinned versions, logged seeds, captured traces

Key framework · Five-part anatomy

  1. Model — does the reasoning and emits tool calls
  2. Tool set — what the agent can do in the world
  3. Memory — at minimum a rolling context window
  4. Loop — alternates deliberation and action
  5. Termination policy — knows when to stop

Discussion prompts

  • Which component is most often mistaken for the entire agent?
  • What does a termination policy look like for an agent with no natural 'done' state?

Opening case

Remember the refund agent? It invented a refund policy instead of telling the customer it wasn't confident. It was missing an organ: the termination check that would have forced it to say “I don't know” before anything else.

Textbook foundation

The five-part anatomy — model, tool set, memory, loop, and termination policy — is the organizing frame of Caldwell, Chapter 3.

Enterprise lens · Addison Boyer

  • Production systems pin model versions, log seeds, and keep traces of the exact messages sent. If you can't replay a run, you can't debug it.
  • Make the termination policy code, not prose: max steps, max spend, wall-clock limit, and an explicit 'cannot complete' exit.
  • In code review, I look for the loop's exit conditions first. They tell me more about an agent's safety than its prompt does.
  • I've watched a model call a one-argument calculator tool with two invented operands. Validate inputs before executing, and return typed errors (a success flag plus “customer email must be a valid email address”), never a raw stack trace.

When Not to Build an Agent

Agents are a Swiss Army knife. Sometimes you only need the screwdriver.

Agents become the default answer for the wrong reasons: demo bias, vendor marketing, and résumé appeal. This module gives you a disciplined four-question gate and a ladder of cheaper alternatives — function calls, classifiers, structured extraction, workflows — with the cost, latency, and accuracy trade-offs of each.

Track

Script · 3 min track · Track 04Know When to Unplug7 scenes · 30 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is track four: Know When to Unplug.

Today's most valuable skill might be recognizing when an agent is the wrong answer.

Scene 2 · Why agents get picked
The wrong reasons
On screen
  • Demo bias
  • Vendor marketing
  • Résumé appeal
  • They feel general — like a Swiss Army knife

Agents become the default answer for reasons that have nothing to do with the problem.

They look more impressive in a demo than a simple classifier.

Model providers market the products that make them money.

And agent sounds great on a résumé.

Agents are a Swiss Army knife. Sometimes you only need the screwdriver, but you carry the cost of the scissors and the toothpick too.

Scene 3 · The decision rule
Four questions before you build
On screen
  • Is the trajectory open-ended?
  • Do inputs vary beyond what a schema captures?
  • Is the output space itself open?
  • Is there genuine action in the world?

Ask four questions.

Is the trajectory open-ended, so you can't know the steps in advance? Research, yes. Classification, no.

Do the inputs vary in ways a schema can't capture?

Is the output space open, rather than one of a few labels or a fixed object?

And is there genuine action in the world, interleaved with observation?

If all four aren't clearly yes, stop and look for something simpler.

Scene 4 · Cheaper alternatives
Climb the ladder slowly
On screen
  • Function call: input X → output Y
  • Prompted classifier: cheap to build
  • Fine-tuned or trained classifier: cheap to run
  • Workflow engine: you own the plan

Here's the ladder of alternatives.

A single function call with structured output handles any task where input X becomes output Y, like extracting entities or summarizing an email.

A prompted classifier is cheap to build but costs more to run.

A fine-tuned model or a traditional classifier is expensive to build and cheap to run.

And a classifier's accuracy ceiling is visible from the outside, in a confusion matrix.

Scene 5 · From the field · Addison Boyer
A healthcare workflow — not an agent
On screen
  • Eligibility → enrollment → enrollment review
  • Decomposed at design time
  • LLMs inside steps (e.g., read an insurance card)
  • No agent loop: it's orchestration

Here's a real example from Addison's work in the healthcare industry.

A program enrollment process has three steps: check eligibility, enroll, then review the enrollment.

Because the steps could be decomposed at design time, it's a workflow.

Models still help inside the steps. At review, one can check whether an uploaded image is really an insurance card, and extract its text.

But there's no agent loop. It's a straight shot, known in advance. That's orchestration, and that's fine.

Reach for an agent when the plan can only be made after the model sees the context, and you can't enumerate the possible plans.

Scene 6 · Enterprise lens
On screen
Ask for ten real inputs and the ideal outputs. If the outputs have a fixed shape, it's a function call.

From the enterprise side: when someone asks for an agent, ask for ten real inputs and the outputs they want.

Half the time, the outputs have a fixed shape. That's a function call, not an agent.

Before switching, run both systems side by side on real traffic and review the disagreements by hand.

And if breaking a rule would cause a production incident, put that rule in code or a re-injected constraint, not deep in a long prompt.

On screen

Here's the map for this module.

Next, we open up the model itself, and the tools it calls. See you there.

Question bank · 3 questions · answer keyQuiz questions for this moduleStarting points — write your own each semester
Write your own each semester. Use these as a starting point, not as the quiz. Each semester you teach, write tailored questions in your own quiz style — your format (multiple choice, short answer, scenario, code reading), your examples from that term's discussions and labs, and fresh scenarios and distractors — so the quiz fits your teaching and old answers don't carry over between terms. This week's graded quiz: Quiz 2 — The Anatomy of an Agent — give it in class, unannounced.

  1. Which signal most strongly suggests a problem will benefit from an agentic approach?

    1. Every output is one of five known labels.That is classification: one model call.
    2. Every input follows the same fixed steps.That is a workflow.
    3. The path is open-ended and each next action depends on what was just observed.Right. Adaptive trajectories are what agents are for.
    4. All possible answers can be listed in advance.Then a lookup or classifier will do.

  2. Why does an agent usually cost more than a workflow that solves the same task?

    1. Agents require a GPU.Hosting is the same either way.
    2. It makes a variable number of model and tool calls per task, so cost and latency are higher and less predictable.Right. That trade-off is the core of 'when not to build an agent'.
    3. Agents cannot cache anything.They can; caching just does not remove the extra calls.
    4. Workflows do not use LLMs.Workflows often include LLM steps, just fixed ones.

  3. What role does the Observation play in a Thought → Action → Observation cycle?

    1. It replaces the original goal.The goal stays fixed.
    2. It tells the model what the last action actually did, so it can choose the next one.Right. Observations close the feedback loop.
    3. It guarantees the previous action succeeded.Observations often report failure; that is the point.
    4. It permanently saves results for future sessions.That is a memory system's job, not the observation's.

Scene 1 · Opening

This is lab track three: Road Case.

Lab two asked, does the loop work? Lab three asks, does it keep working?

Scene 2 · The stress test
On screen
Longer tasks, more tools, and a model that changes under you.

You'll take your lab two agent and stress it: longer conversations, more tool calls, and a bigger step budget.

You'll run it two ways: online through OpenRouter, and offline against a local model served by llama dot c p p.

And you'll tier it: a cheap model drives tool selection, and an expensive model writes only the final answer.

Scene 3 · Failure modes
Defend against what goes wrong at scale
On screen
  • Context saturation → windowed summaries
  • Instruction drift → re-inject constraints
  • Confabulation → structured outputs
  • Silent tools → fail loudly

As context grows, details in the middle get lost. Summarize older turns in a window, so the context stays bounded.

Critical rules fade over a long run. Re-inject them on every step.

Models invent arguments with confidence. Enforce a schema on every tool call, online and offline.

And design tools that fail loudly, with an explicit error, instead of quietly returning an empty result.

Scene 4 · Measure it
Observability and drift
On screen
  • Log every tool call
  • Schemas a junior engineer could follow
  • Pinned model vs. model actually served
  • Latency, tokens, run-to-run variance

Log every tool call as a structured record: the tool, the arguments, the result, and the time it took.

Write tool names and descriptions so clear that a junior engineer, or a small model, gets them right the first time.

Check which model actually answered. Pinning a version in configuration doesn't guarantee it's the one being served.

Then measure latency, token cost, and how much the answers vary from run to run, on the same prompt.

Core Capabilities

The model, its tools, its memory, its plans, and the protocol that connects them.

Module 5 · Week 5 · Reading Ch. 5–6 Check passed

LLMs as Reasoning Engines & Tools as Contracts

The model proposes; the tool contract decides what actually happens.

A modern agent's model is an instruction-tuned, tool-use–trained LLM with implicit objectives you didn't set and can't inspect — and the provider can change it any time. We treat it as a black-box reasoning engine, evaluate models on your own task evidence, and then design tool schemas that make correct use easy and dangerous use impossible.

Track

Script · 2 min track · Track 05Tuning the Instrument6 scenes · 20 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is track five: Tuning the Instrument.

We'll look at the model as a reasoning engine, and the tools as contracts that decide what actually happens.

Scene 2 · How tool-using models are made
Four training stages
On screen
  • Pre-training: language and world facts
  • Instruction tuning: act like an assistant
  • Tool-use training: know when to call a tool
  • Alignment: reward accurate, safe tool use

Today's agent models are almost always instruction-tuned language models with tool-use support.

Pre-training on huge amounts of text teaches language, reasoning patterns, and facts.

Instruction tuning teaches the model to act like an assistant instead of an autocomplete.

Tool-use training teaches it to recognize when it lacks information and to emit a precise tool call.

And alignment rewards accurate, safe tool use, and penalizes guessing.

Scene 3 · Big idea
On screen
Treating the model as deterministic is the most common mistake in agent projects.

Here's the big idea.

The model has implicit objectives shaped by training you didn't run and can't inspect, and the provider can update it at any time.

So treat it as a black box with an interface: messages and tool definitions go in, text or a tool call comes out.

Your engineering question is what you can reliably cause it to do, and what you can't.

Scene 4 · Evaluate models on your task
Before you switch models
On screen
  • 30–100 held-out, realistic inputs
  • Happy paths, edge cases, known failures
  • Track tokens, cache hits, steps, retries
  • Check current pricing before go-live

Benchmarks are not your task. Build a held-out set of thirty to a hundred realistic inputs.

Include happy paths, edge cases, and failures you already know about.

Trade off cost, latency, and quality with evidence, tracking tokens, cache behavior, step counts, and retries.

Scene 5 · Chapter 6
Tools are contracts
On screen
  • Narrow, explicit, versioned schemas
  • Say what the tool does NOT do
  • Retryable vs. terminal errors
  • Idempotency keys on every write

Tool-use quality is bounded by the quality of your tool definitions.

Keep schemas narrow, explicit, and versioned.

In one case, a single added sentence describing what a tool does not do eliminated an entire class of production bugs.

Tell the caller whether an error is retryable or terminal, and protect every write with an idempotency key so a retry can't do it twice.

On screen

Quiz

Question bank · 3 questions · answer keyQuiz questions for this moduleStarting points — write your own each semester
Write your own each semester. Use these as a starting point, not as the quiz. Each semester you teach, write tailored questions in your own quiz style — your format (multiple choice, short answer, scenario, code reading), your examples from that term's discussions and labs, and fresh scenarios and distractors — so the quiz fits your teaching and old answers don't carry over between terms.

  1. A tool returns: "Invalid date format: expected YYYY-MM-DD." How should the agent treat this error?

    1. Transient: retry the same call with backoff.Retrying the same bad argument will fail the same way.
    2. Input error: fix the argument and call again.Right. The message says exactly what to change.
    3. Fatal: stop the whole run.Too drastic for a fixable argument.
    4. Ignore it and answer from memory.That is how confabulation starts.

  2. An agent sometimes calls create_ticket with priority set to the literal text of the field's description. What is the best fix?

    1. Switch to a bigger model.Expensive, and it does not remove the ambiguity.
    2. Make priority optional.Hides the problem and loses data.
    3. Constrain priority to an enum and say in the description what to do when it is unknown.Right. Tools are contracts: tighten the schema and spell out the escape hatch.
    4. Add unit tests for create_ticket.The tool works; the model's call is what is wrong.

  3. Which situation most favors fine-tuning over prompting?

    1. The output format will change next month.You would have to retrain every time it changes.
    2. A narrow, stable task run at high volume, with roughly 1,000 labeled examples.Right. Stable schema, volume, and data are the conditions that pay for fine-tuning.
    3. A prototype with 20 examples.Not enough data and too early.
    4. An open-ended research assistant.Broad tasks are better served by a strong base model and good prompts.

LabLab 4 — Tool RoutingA meta-tool that picks the toolset before the agent runs.Open
Script · 2 min track · Lab Track 4Stage Manager5 scenes · 15 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is lab track four: Stage Manager.

Before the show starts, someone decides who's on stage. Today you build that someone.

Scene 2 · The problem
On screen
Every tool on every call costs tokens, and invites the wrong pick.

As an agent gains tools, every request carries every tool definition, and the model has more ways to choose wrong.

The fix is a routing step. Before the agent runs, a cheap model reads the request and picks which toolsets it needs.

You'll build it as a meta tool called get available tools. It does no work for the user. It only decides what the real work will need.

Scene 3 · The router
Classify, then hand over a toolset
On screen
  • Four domains: calendar · email · files · billing
  • Plus none, for no tools
  • Force the classification with tool_choice
  • Return domains and their tools

There are four toolset domains, calendar, email, files, and billing, plus none, for requests that need no tools.

One request can touch several domains, so the router returns a list.

Use tool choice to force the model to call the classifier, instead of replying in prose.

Then return the chosen domains, and the tool names that belong to them.

Scene 4 · Enums, not descriptions
Constrain it, then check it
On screen
  • A JSON Schema enum lists the valid values
  • A description is only a hint
  • Validate with jsonschema anyway
  • Fall back safely when it's invalid

Constrain the output with a JSON schema enum: a fixed list of valid values, where case and spelling count.

Listing the values in a description isn't enough. A description is a hint the model may ignore.

Even with an enum, validate the result in your own code. Some backends treat the schema as a suggestion, and small local models drift.

If the output won't parse, fails validation, or comes back empty, fall back to a safe default.

Memory: Working, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural

A brilliant agent with amnesia is still frustrating to work with.

An analyst agent was excellent on day one — but users had to re-explain their competitive landscape every session, and usage fell 60% in two weeks. Adding a memory layer didn't make it smarter; it made it something you could have a continuing relationship with. This module covers the four memory types, the stores that serve them, and the failure modes that appear after months in production.

Track

Script · 2 min track · Track 06Muscle Memory6 scenes · 21 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is track six: Muscle Memory.

A brilliant agent with amnesia is still frustrating to work with. Today we fix that.

Scene 2 · Opening case
On screen
After two weeks, usage dropped sixty percent.

An analyst agent was excellent on day one.

But every session, users had to re-explain their competitors, their preferred frameworks, and their open research threads.

After two weeks, usage dropped sixty percent. Starting from scratch was more frustrating than the agent was useful.

Adding a memory layer didn't make it smarter. It made it something you could have a continuing relationship with.

Scene 3 · Chapter 7 framework
Four types of memory
On screen
  • Working — what the model attends to now
  • Episodic — what happened in past sessions
  • Semantic — facts that don't expire
  • Procedural — routines learned over time

Following Caldwell's chapter seven, there are four kinds of memory.

Working memory is what the model is attending to right now.

Episodic memory is what happened in past sessions.

Semantic memory holds facts and knowledge that don't expire.

And procedural memory is the routines an agent accumulates over the lifetime of its deployment.

Scene 4 · Storage
Match the store to the memory
On screen
  • Key-value: fast-changing session state
  • Vector + keyword (hybrid) search
  • Graphs for relationship questions
  • Start simple; add stores on evidence

Each memory type wants a different store.

Fast-changing session state, like the current project or the tool-call count, fits a key-value store.

For recall, hybrid search, combining vector similarity with keyword search, beats pure vector search on most production tasks.

And when the question is about relationships, like competitors, board members, or subsidiaries, reach for a graph.

Scene 5 · Enterprise lens
What breaks after months
On screen
  • Overlapping, duplicate summaries
  • Stale facts that conflict with live data
  • Names, affiliations, financial data
  • Retention and deletion are requirements

Here's what shows up after months in production.

A user who asks about the same company in ten sessions leaves ten overlapping summaries. Design consolidation from day one.

Memory also accumulates names, affiliations, and financial data. Retention, tenancy boundaries, and deletion are requirements, not features.

And add stores only when production evidence justifies the cost, not because the diagram looks elegant.

Scene 6 · Closing
On screen
The finished board — the module map.

Here's the map for this module.

Reading

Required reading · Caldwell, Chapter 7Memory: Short-term, Long-term, Episodic, SemanticThe Agentic AI BibleGo
Reading outline · Ch. 7

Start simple. Add memory stores only when production evidence justifies the operational cost — not because the architecture diagram looks elegant.

  1. Working memory
    • Current context window
    • Session state (KV store)
  2. Episodic memory
    • Past sessions & outcomes
    • Timestamped summaries
  3. Semantic memory
    • Stable facts & preferences
    • ~80% of data is unstructured
  4. Procedural memory
    • Learned routines
    • Accumulates over deployment
  5. Retrieval
    • Hybrid: vector + BM25
    • Graphs for relationships
  6. Production failures
    • Duplicate, stale summaries
    • PII & sensitive data

The short-term / long-term / episodic / semantic memory taxonomy and the memory-store architectures follow Caldwell, Chapter 7. Outline written for this course; assign the chapter itself.

Write your own each semester. Use these as a starting point, not as the quiz. Each semester you teach, write tailored questions in your own quiz style — your format (multiple choice, short answer, scenario, code reading), your examples from that term's discussions and labs, and fresh scenarios and distractors — so the quiz fits your teaching and old answers don't carry over between terms. This week's graded quiz: Quiz 3 — Models, Tools, and Memory — give it in class, unannounced.

  1. Which type of memory lives in the system prompt and its few-shot examples?

    1. WorkingWorking memory is whatever the context window currently holds.
    2. EpisodicEpisodic memory records past sessions.
    3. SemanticSemantic memory stores long-lived facts.
    4. ProceduralRight. It encodes how the agent should reason and act in every session.

  2. A travel agent's prompt says never to book over $2,000 without approval. After a long, pushy conversation it books $2,600 on its own. What is the failure, and the fix?

    1. Context saturation; use a bigger context window.A bigger window would make the rule even easier to bury.
    2. Instruction drift; reinject the rule as a constraint on every step, and enforce it in code.Right. Long contexts dilute early instructions, so keep the constraint current and enforce it outside the model.
    3. Tool schema drift; add an enum.The schema was not the problem.
    4. Nothing is wrong; users can override rules.Policy is not negotiable by conversation.

  3. Where should a fact like "the company's fiscal year starts in July" be stored?

    1. Working memoryIt would vanish when the context is cleared.
    2. Episodic memoryIt is not a record of a past session.
    3. Semantic memoryRight. It is a durable fact about the world.
    4. Nowhere; the model already knows it.The model cannot know your company's facts.

Script · 2 min track · Project Track · MidtermEncore6 scenes · 19 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is the project track for your midterm: Encore.

A music agent that sits on top of your own ListenBrainz account, and remembers.

Scene 2 · One request, start to finish
On screen
Make me a forty-minute focus playlist like last week's, but nothing I've played lately.

Encore answers questions about your listening, finds music, builds playlists in your account, and exports them to a streaming service.

For a request like this one, it recalls last week's session, checks your recent listens, finds candidates, and verifies every recording is real.

Then it creates the playlist and exports it, and both of those writes wait for your approval.

Your code never scripts that sequence. The model chooses each step after reading the last result.

Scene 3 · Built on your labs
A real agent, against real APIs
On screen
  • Bounded ReAct loop, at most 12 steps
  • About 20 tools with JSON schemas
  • Typed results and an error taxonomy
  • Approval gates on every write

Encore reuses your bounded loop, your lab three hardening, and your lab four router.

It has about twenty tools, across listening, the music catalog, discovery, your library, and memory.

Every tool returns a typed result, and errors are observations too, so the model can try something else.

And anything that changes your account waits for approval, with rate limits and timeouts around every call.

Scene 4 · Chapter 7
Four kinds of memory
On screen
  • Working — this conversation
  • Episodic — past sessions
  • Semantic — how ListenBrainz works
  • Procedural — Encore's own rules

What makes Encore more than a chatbot is memory, all four kinds from track six.

Working memory holds this conversation. Episodic memory recalls the one from last week.

Semantic memory knows how ListenBrainz and its exports work. Procedural memory follows Encore's rules, like never exporting without approval.

Add a retention policy, a way to delete everything about a user, and defenses against stale or polluted memories.

Scene 5 · Prove it
Evaluate, then present
On screen
  • Evaluate retrieval before the agent
  • Held-out requests
  • Accuracy · latency · cost · variance
  • Present your evidence

Evaluate your retrieval first: chunking, recall, and hybrid search, before you build the agent layer on top.

Then test the whole agent on held-out requests, and measure accuracy, latency, cost, and run-to-run variance.

There are two workshop checkpoints along the way, and you'll present your Encore, with its evidence, to the class.

On screen
The finished board — the module map.

Here's the project on one board.

Build it well. Your final project starts from this code.

Teaching notes

Learning objectives

  • Differentiate working, episodic, semantic, and procedural memory
  • Match vector, keyword/hybrid, graph, and key-value stores to memory needs
  • Design write, deduplication, and retention policies
  • Anticipate long-term failure modes: staleness, overlap, sensitive data

Key framework · Four types of memory

  1. Working — what the model attends to right now
  2. Episodic — what happened in past sessions
  3. Semantic — facts and knowledge that don't expire
  4. Procedural — routines learned over a deployment's lifetime

Discussion prompts

  • Which memories should never become prompt context?
  • How should an agent resolve a recalled fact that conflicts with the live system?

Opening case

Analysts re-explained competitors, preferred frameworks, and open research threads at the start of every conversation. After two weeks, usage dropped 60%. The fix: preferences and open threads stored in a vector database keyed by analyst, retrieved at the start of each session.

Textbook foundation

The short-term / long-term / episodic / semantic memory taxonomy and the memory-store architectures follow Caldwell, Chapter 7.

Enterprise lens · Addison Boyer

  • Hybrid search (vector similarity + BM25 keyword) should be your default; most production vector databases support it natively.
  • A user who asks about the same company in ten sessions over three months leaves ten overlapping summaries. Design consolidation from day one.
  • Memory accumulates names, affiliations, and financial data. Retention, tenancy boundaries, and deletion are requirements, not features.

Planning & Decomposition

Turn an open-ended goal into a tractable, budgeted sequence of actions.

A quarterly-planning agent worked on small inputs but failed on every list longer than four or five initiatives — it spent twenty steps on the first initiative and ran out of attention for the rest. A 200-token planning step fixed it. We compare four planning strategies and show how production systems blend them.

Track

Script · 2 min track · Track 07The Setlist5 scenes · 18 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is track seven: The Setlist.

Every good show starts with a plan. So does every agent that has more than one thing to do.

Scene 2 · Opening case
On screen
Twenty steps deep on initiative one — and no attention left for the rest.

A planning agent was asked to research a list of engineering initiatives and produce a prioritized roadmap.

With four or five initiatives, it was fine. With more, it failed every time.

It followed a chain of dependencies on the first initiative for twenty steps, and never got to the others.

The fix was a planning step: list the initiatives, what to learn about each, and a step budget for each. About two hundred tokens and one extra call.

Scene 3 · Chapter 8 framework
Four planning strategies
On screen
  • ReAct — think, act, observe, interleaved
  • Plan-and-Execute — plan up front
  • Reflexion — revise after failure
  • Tree-of-Thoughts — explore alternatives

Following Caldwell's chapter eight, there are four planning strategies.

ReAct interleaves thought, action, and observation. It's fluid, but it drifts without budgets.

Plan-and-Execute writes the plan up front and executes it step by step, which makes checkpoints easy.

Reflexion revises the plan in response to failure.

And Tree-of-Thoughts explores several plans in parallel, when being wrong is expensive.

Scene 4 · Enterprise lens
Planning in production
On screen
  • Plan, execute a step, verify
  • Replan only on real deviation
  • Reflect when a tool fails or a validator rejects
  • Persist the plan

In production, these get blended.

Propose a plan, execute one step, verify it, and replan only when an observation meaningfully changes the picture.

Reflection fires per step, when a tool call fails or a validator rejects output, not by replaying whole episodes.

Tree-of-Thoughts needs a judge to pick a branch, and that judge is another probabilistic model. Test the judge.

And persist the plan. A plan that lives only in the context window can't be audited, resumed, or reviewed.

Scene 5 · Closing
On screen
The finished board — the module map.

Here's the map for this module.

This week's lab is a midterm workshop. Bring your Encore agent and your questions.

Reading

Required reading · Caldwell, Chapter 8Planning and DecompositionThe Agentic AI BibleGo
Reading outline · Ch. 8

Planning is cheap insurance against an agent spending its whole budget on the first interesting thing it finds.

  1. ReAct
    • Fluid exploration
    • Drifts without budgets
  2. Plan-and-Execute
    • Upfront plan
    • Checkpoint each step
  3. Reflexion
    • Learn from failure
    • Fires on tool error / rejection
  4. Tree-of-Thoughts
    • Parallel alternatives
    • LLM-as-judge problem
  5. Hybrid in production
    • Plan, execute, verify
    • Replan on real deviation
  6. Budgets
    • Per-item step budget
    • Cheap: ~200 tokens

  1. Why is a numbered markdown list often preferred over a strict JSON object for an agent's plan?

    1. JSON cannot hold a step's status.It can, easily.
    2. Markdown plans never need updating.Plans are updated constantly during execution.
    3. It is legible to both the model and your code: models write it reliably, and a few lines of code can parse it.Right. One artifact serves both readers.
    4. JSON cannot be put back into the context.It can; it is just noisier for the model.

  2. The same failure keeps triggering the same reflection across many sessions. Where should that lesson go?

    1. Working memoryIt would have to be rediscovered every session.
    2. Episodic memory, as another stored sessionThat just records the failure again.
    3. Procedural memory, as a rule in the system prompt or tool descriptionRight. Recurring lessons should become standing instructions.
    4. Semantic memory, as a fact about the worldIt is guidance about behavior, not a world fact.

  3. Why is Tree-of-Thoughts the wrong default for most agent tasks?

    1. It cannot use tools.It can.
    2. Its cost multiplies: candidates × scoring calls × depth.Right. Reserve it for problems where search actually pays off.
    3. It only works on arithmetic.It is general, just expensive.
    4. It cannot be combined with other strategies.It can be combined.

  • Compare ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, Reflexion, and Tree-of-Thoughts
  • Distinguish academic framing from production implementation

Key framework · Four planning strategies

  1. ReAct — thought → action → observation, interleaved
  2. Plan-and-Execute — upfront plan, sequential execution
  3. Reflexion — revise the plan in response to failure
  4. Tree-of-Thoughts — explore alternative plans in parallel

Enterprise lens · Addison Boyer

  • Academic Reflexion re-runs whole episodes. In production I fire per-step reflection only when a tool call fails or a validator rejects output.
  • Tree-of-Thoughts needs a judge to pick a branch — and that judge is another probabilistic model. Budget for it, and test the judge.
  • Persist the plan. A plan that lives only in the context window can't be audited, resumed, or reviewed by a human.

Model Context Protocol (MCP)

MCP standardizes the envelope — not the contents.

MCP is pitched as 'the USB-C of AI' that 'lets any agent talk to any tool'. Those framings are wrong in a specific way that matters for design. MCP is a JSON-RPC 2.0 wire format with a small standard library of messages for tool discovery, invocation, resources, and prompt templates. It moves integration cost from the wire format to the semantic layer — where it always belonged.

Track

Script · 2 min track · Track 08Plug and Play?6 scenes · 19 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is track eight: Plug and Play?

Notice the question mark. Today we look at the Model Context Protocol, and at what it does and doesn't promise.

Scene 2 · Big idea
On screen
MCP standardizes the envelope, not the contents.

You'll hear MCP called the USB-C of AI, a protocol that lets any agent talk to any tool.

Those framings are wrong in a way that matters for design.

MCP is a JSON-RPC wire format with a small standard library of messages for discovering and calling tools, reading resources, and looking up prompt templates.

It's to agent tools what HTTP is to documents. A shared envelope, not shared meaning.

Scene 3 · Chapter 9 framework
MCP building blocks
On screen
  • Host → client → server
  • Initialize and negotiate capabilities
  • Tools · resources · prompts
  • Transports: stdio and Streamable HTTP

Following Caldwell's chapter nine, a host coordinates a client that talks to one or more servers.

The connection starts with initialization, where both sides negotiate versions and capabilities.

Servers expose tools you call, resources you read, and prompts you reuse.

And messages travel over standard input and output for local servers, or Streamable HTTP for remote ones.

Scene 4 · Why it matters
Integration cost moved to the right place
On screen
  • Before: a different tool format per framework
  • After: one envelope everyone speaks
  • Still yours: the domain model
  • Servers crash — clients must expect it

Before MCP, each framework solved tool connectivity its own way. Three years of bespoke abstractions.

MCP fixed the envelope. But an MCP server for a customer platform still has to understand that platform's domain model.

It moved integration cost from the wire format, where it never belonged, to the semantic layer, where it always did.

Scene 5 · Enterprise lens
Production-grade MCP
On screen
  • Audit-log every tool call
  • Transports don't authorize anything
  • Scope credentials per server
  • Expose only what this user and task need

From the enterprise side: audit logging on every tool call is what separates a production server from a development server.

It's your forensic record for security incidents, and your best source for debugging.

Transports move bytes. They don't authorize anything. Enforce permissions in the host and the server.

And only enable capabilities the current user and task actually need. A long tool catalog is an attack surface.

On screen

  1. An MCP server reads files on the user's laptop with the user's own credentials, for one agent on the same machine. Which transport fits?

    1. Streamable HTTP behind a load balancerThere is nothing to scale, and now you have a network service to secure.

    3. HTTP + SSEBuilt for remote streaming, not local subprocesses.
    4. It does not matter.Transport affects security and operations.

    1. ToolsTools perform actions with possible side effects.
    2. ResourcesRight. Resources are addressable context to read.
    3. PromptsPrompts are reusable templates the server offers.
    4. TransportsA transport is how messages move, not a capability.

  3. A team wants one MCP server shared by many users' agents across the company. Which transport fits best?

    1. stdiostdio only works for a local subprocess.
    2. Streamable HTTP, deployed as a remote service with authenticationRight. Remote, multi-client, scalable.
    3. Copying the server to every laptopThen you have N servers to patch.
    4. EmailNot an MCP transport.

Part III

Architecture and Patterns

Structuring single agents, coordinating many, keeping humans in charge, and running for hours or days.

Module 9 · Week 9 · Reading Ch. 10 Check passed

Single-Agent Patterns

Not more capable — more organized.

A support agent ran well for six months, then — with no change to model, tools, or prompt — began offering refunds on unverified orders, skipping steps, and looping on the same tool call. The cause was a single flat ReAct loop meeting scale. Separating routing from execution and adding explicit state fixed all three failure modes within a week.

Track

Script · 2 min track · Track 09Solo Practice5 scenes · 21 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is track nine: Solo Practice.

Before forming a band, learn to play well alone. Today is about structuring a single agent.

Scene 2 · Opening case
On screen
Nothing changed — not the model, the tools, or the prompt. Then it started failing.

A customer support agent ran well for six months.

Then, at higher volume, it started offering refunds on unverified orders, skipping steps, and calling the same tool three or four times in a row.

Nobody had changed the model, the tools, or the prompt.

The failures came from context growth, tool complexity, and a new mix of requests, all hitting one flat loop.

Separating routing from execution, and tracking state between steps, fixed all three within a week. It didn't get more capable. It got more organized.

Scene 3 · Chapter 10 framework
Core single-agent patterns
On screen
  • Router → executor
  • Validator wrapper
  • Step machine with explicit state
  • Scratchpad with an explicit plan
  • Explicit, tested escalation

Following Caldwell's chapter ten, here are the core patterns.

A router classifies the request, then hands it to an executor with a smaller, focused toolset.

A validator checks outputs before they leave, using schemas, tests, or a second model.

A step machine makes states and transitions explicit, like an onboarding flow that must collect certain fields before creating an account.

A scratchpad gives the agent a written plan it keeps outside the conversation: the steps, what's done, and what it has learned so far.

Your code re-injects the scratchpad on every step, and the agent checks items off as it goes, so a long task doesn't lose its place in a growing context.

And escalation is a real code path: when the agent can't finish safely, it hands the case to a person.

Most production agents combine two or three of these.

Scene 4 · Enterprise lens
Add structure on evidence
On screen
  • Start with a flat ReAct loop
  • Add a pattern for a failure you've seen
  • Validators: the minimum that catches it
  • Escalation: in code and in tests

The flat loop is still the right place to start.

Add a pattern only when production evidence shows the failure it prevents.

Keep validators to the minimum needed to catch failures you've actually seen. Every check costs latency.

And if an escalation path isn't in the code, and covered by a test, it doesn't exist.

Quiz

Question bank · 3 questions · answer keyQuiz questions for this moduleStarting points — write your own each semester
Write your own each semester. Use these as a starting point, not as the quiz. Each semester you teach, write tailored questions in your own quiz style — your format (multiple choice, short answer, scenario, code reading), your examples from that term's discussions and labs, and fresh scenarios and distractors — so the quiz fits your teaching and old answers don't carry over between terms.

  1. A support agent with 15 tools picks the wrong tool more often as the conversation grows. What most directly fixes this?

    1. Longer tool descriptions in one big promptMore text makes the selection problem harder.
    2. A lightweight router that classifies the request and dispatches it to an executor with only the relevant toolsRight. Shrink the choice set before the model has to choose.
    3. Retrieve tool docs but keep all 15 tools attachedThe full tool set is still there to confuse it.
    4. Let it pick, then check and retryThat treats the symptom, not the cause.

  2. An onboarding agent must collect four required fields before creating an account. Which pattern stops it from skipping steps?

    1. A checklist in the promptThe model can still skip it.
    2. A stateful step machine where your code tracks the phase and checks completion criteriaRight. Make the sequence structural, not optional.
    3. Four agents that each decide independentlyAdds coordination problems.
    4. Review after the account is createdToo late.

  3. Which is the best use of a validator-as-wrapper for a strict policy rule?

    1. A general quality scoreIt never checks the specific rule.
    2. Check the response against the rule, allow a bounded number of revisions, then escalate if it still failsRight. Specific check, bounded retries, clear exit.
    3. Validate after the user has already seen the responseThe violation has already happened.
    4. Let the validator rewrite with no limitNo bound means no guarantee of termination.

Teaching notes

Learning objectives

  • Choose among router, validator, step-machine, and scratchpad patterns
  • Keep policy and tool authority outside model prose
  • Combine patterns — most production agents use two or three
  • Know when a single agent is no longer enough

Key framework · Core single-agent patterns

  1. Router → executor: classify, then act
  2. Validator wrapper: check outputs before release
  3. Step machine: explicit states and guarded transitions
  4. Escalation path: explicit, coded, and tested

Discussion prompts

  • What does the validator know that the executor doesn't?
  • At what point is a move to multiple agents defensible?

Opening case

Returns, refunds, product questions: fine at low volume. At scale, context growth plus tool-set complexity plus a new request distribution produced unverified refunds, skipped steps, and 3–4× repeated tool calls. The fix wasn't a better model; it was structure.

Textbook foundation

The named single-agent architecture patterns and their trade-offs in complexity follow Caldwell, Chapter 10.

Enterprise lens · Addison Boyer

  • A validator should be the minimum needed to catch failure modes you've actually seen — not a wish list. Every check costs latency.
  • If an escalation path isn't in the code and covered by a test, it doesn't exist.
  • Behavior that 'emerges at scale' is still a design bug. Load-test with a realistic request distribution, not ten hand-picked prompts.

Multi-Agent Systems & Shared Infrastructure

Agents talking to each other isn't an architecture. Typed messages and shared state are.

A legal-tech 'AI Paralegal Pipeline' looked clean on paper — extract, research, draft — but failed on hundred-page document sets where the extractor couldn't know in advance what the researcher would need. We compare supervisor-worker, pipeline, parallel fan-out, and hierarchical patterns, then build the shared infrastructure every multi-agent deployment needs.

Track

Script · 2 min track · Track 10Forming the Band6 scenes · 19 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is track ten: Forming the Band.

Agents talking to each other isn't an architecture. Today we look at what is.

Scene 2 · Opening case
On screen
The extractor couldn't know in advance what the researcher would need.

A legal technology company built a paralegal pipeline: extract facts, research precedent, draft.

On paper it was clean. On document sets hundreds of pages long, it failed.

Connecting facts to precedent required understanding the extraction step couldn't produce up front, and mismatched schemas between stages made it worse.

Scene 3 · Chapter 11 patterns
Ways to organize a band
On screen
  • Supervisor and workers
  • Pipeline of stages
  • Parallel fan-out
  • Hierarchies — usually two levels

Following Caldwell's chapter eleven, there are a few common patterns.

A supervisor assigns work to specialized workers and combines the results.

A pipeline passes work through explicit stages.

Parallel fan-out suits independent tasks, like the same research run against many companies.

Hierarchies can go deep, but most production systems settle at two levels: one supervisor, several workers.

Scene 4 · Shared infrastructure
What every band needs
On screen
  • Shared state with locks or optimistic concurrency
  • Typed, versioned, validated messages
  • First result wins (Redis SETNX)
  • Explicit ownership and bounded fan-out

Whatever the pattern, the same infrastructure shows up.

Shared state needs locking or optimistic concurrency, or two agents will overwrite each other's work.

Messages between agents need schemas both sides agree on, with versions.

And retries need idempotency. With an atomic set-if-not-exists, only the first agent to finish a task records its result.

Scene 5 · Enterprise lens
On screen
Mismatched schemas between stages are the most common source of pipeline failures.

From the enterprise side: version every message contract.

Mismatched schemas between stages cause more pipeline failures than anything else.

Multiple agents multiply both specialization and coordination risk. Spend your effort on shared state and recovery, not role-play.

    • Independent documents
    • Same task, many companies

    • Stage schema mismatch

Enterprise lens · Addison Boyer

  • Mismatched schemas between stages are the most common source of pipeline failures I see. Version every message contract.
  • Most production hierarchies stabilize at two levels — one supervisor, several workers. Deeper trees are usually a smell.
  • Use atomic operations (Redis SETNX) so that a retried worker can't overwrite a task another worker already completed.

Human-in-the-Loop & Human-on-the-Loop

Place oversight by the risk of the action — not the difficulty of the task.

A fraud-detection agent deployed fully autonomously was right on 85% of clear cases — but on the ambiguous 15%, human reviewers disagreed with it nearly half the time. The agent didn't know when it was outside its reliable range, and neither did the team. The fix changed the interaction model: decide above a confidence threshold, escalate below it with a one-click approve / modify / reject.

Track

Script · 3 min track · Track 11The Mixing Desk7 scenes · 27 narration lines
Scene 1 · Opening

This is track eleven: The Mixing Desk.

Every band needs someone at the board with approve, modify, and reject buttons. Today, that's the human.

Scene 2 · Opening case
On screen
Right on the clear cases. Confidently wrong on the hard fifteen percent.

A fraud-detection agent was deployed fully autonomously.

It handled the clear eighty-five percent of cases well.

But on the unclear fifteen percent, human reviewers disagreed with it almost half the time.

It didn't know when it was outside its reliable range. Neither did the team.

The fix: decide above a confidence threshold, and below it, escalate with a short explanation a reviewer can approve, modify, or reject in one click.

Scene 3 · Chapter 12 framework
Two oversight models
On screen
  • HITL: agent pauses for a human
  • HOTL: agent proceeds; human monitors
  • Choose by risk, not task difficulty

Following Caldwell's chapter twelve, there are two models.

With a human in the loop, the agent stops and waits for approval before passing a checkpoint. Think payments, external emails, production deploys, or court filings.

With a human on the loop, the agent keeps going, and a person monitors and can intervene. Think high-volume content moderation.

The choice is a risk calculation, not a judgment about how hard the task is.

Scene 4 · Minimum viable HOTL
The smallest real human-on-the-loop
On screen
  • Log every decision, with its reason
  • A review queue: sample, plus low confidence
  • Alerts on thresholds and anomalies
  • A stop button, and a way to undo

So what's the smallest human-on-the-loop system that actually works? Four pieces.

First, the agent logs every action it takes, with a one-line reason, the inputs it used, and its confidence.

Second, a review queue. A person reviews a random sample of decisions, plus every decision below the confidence threshold, after the fact.

Third, alerts. When volume spikes, error rates climb, or reviewers start disagreeing with the agent, someone gets paged.

And fourth, a stop button. One switch pauses the agent, and every action it takes has a known way to be reversed.

Without all four, nobody is really on the loop. They're just hoping.

Scene 5 · Placing intervention points
Three questions, two rules
On screen
  • How reversible is the action?
  • How often is the agent out of range?
  • How costly is the review delay?
  • Rule: before irreversible actions
  • Rule: below a measured confidence

Ask three questions. How reversible is the action? How often does the agent operate outside its reliable range? And how expensive is the delay of a human review?

Then follow two rules.

Place intervention points before irreversible actions, like sending an email, committing a transaction, or deleting data.

And place them where the agent's confidence drops below a threshold you've measured.

Scene 6 · Enterprise lens
Design from the reviewer's chair
On screen
  • A summary, not a raw trace
  • Approve · modify · reject
  • The threshold is a tunable parameter
  • Durable run state across the pause

Design from the reviewer's chair. What do they need to know, and what do they need to be able to do?

Usually that's a concise summary and three buttons, not a raw trace.

Treat the threshold as a tunable parameter. Track how often reviewers agree, and move it with evidence.

And paused runs must survive restarts. Keep run state in a database, and confirm nothing changed before resuming.

On screen

Here's the map for this module.
